title: Amazon FBA Fees Explained in Plain Language
headline: Amazon FBA Fees Explained in Plain Language
description: A plain-language guide to Amazon FBA fees for beginners: referral fees, fulfilment fees, storage, returns, removals and other charges, and how to check the current figures for your own product.
body_html:
Fulfilment by Amazon (FBA) lets you send stock to Amazon's warehouses so that Amazon stores it, packs each order, delivers it and handles most customer service and returns. That convenience has a cost, and the fees are one of the main reasons a product turns out to be more or less profitable than a seller expected. This guide explains the main types of fee in plain language so you know what to look for. It deliberately gives no fixed amounts: Amazon's fees differ by marketplace, category and product size, and they are updated from time to time. Always check the current fee schedule in Seller Central for your own figures.

1. The selling plan fee

Before any product fees, there is the cost of the seller account itself. Most marketplaces offer an individual plan, where you pay a small charge per item sold, and a professional plan, with a monthly subscription. The professional plan is usually needed for advertising, Brand Registry tools and other features most serious sellers use. This fee applies whether you use FBA or ship orders yourself.

2. Referral fees

A referral fee is Amazon's commission on each sale. It is normally a percentage of the total price the customer pays, and the percentage depends on the category. Some categories also have a minimum fee per item. Referral fees are charged on every sale, whether you use FBA or not, so they belong in every margin calculation. Choosing the right category for your product matters, because the same item could carry a different rate in a different category, and Amazon decides which category is correct.

3. FBA fulfilment fees

This is the per-unit fee for picking, packing and delivering an order. It is based mainly on the product's size tier and its shipping weight, which includes the packaging. A small, light product sits in a lower tier. A product that is just a little too long, too wide or too heavy can move into a higher tier and cost noticeably more to fulfil.

  • Measure carefully. Measure the packed product, not the item alone. A slightly smaller box can sometimes keep a product in a cheaper tier.
  • Check what Amazon recorded. Amazon measures products in its warehouses. If its measurements are larger than yours, your fees will be higher. You can review the dimensions on file and ask for a re-check if you think they are wrong.
  • Some products cost more. Items classed as dangerous goods, such as some batteries, aerosols or liquids, can carry different fees and extra paperwork.

4. Storage fees

Amazon charges for the space your stock takes up in its warehouses. Monthly storage fees are usually based on volume rather than the number of units, and they are often higher in the busy months before the end-of-year holidays. Stock that sits unsold for a long time can attract extra charges for aged inventory on top of normal storage. Bulky products that sell slowly are where storage costs grow fastest.

This is why sending too much stock is a common and costly mistake. Plan quantities from real sales, keep an eye on the inventory age reports, and act early on slow stock with a price change, a promotion or a removal.

5. Inbound and shipment-related charges

Getting stock into Amazon's network can involve its own costs. Depending on the marketplace, these can include fees linked to how and where your shipment is placed in the warehouse network, charges for prep or labelling services if Amazon does that work for you, and penalties for problems such as missing labels or poorly packed boxes. Following the packaging and labelling rules exactly is the easiest way to avoid unplanned charges. Your own freight cost to the warehouse is separate and also needs to be in your numbers.

6. Returns, removals and disposals

  • Returns. In some categories, and for products with a high return rate, Amazon may charge a returns processing fee. Returned units that cannot be resold are lost stock as well.
  • Removals and disposals. If you ask Amazon to send stock back to you or to dispose of it, there is a per-unit fee.
  • Refunds. When an order is refunded, Amazon usually returns most of the referral fee but may keep an administration charge.

7. Costs that are not Amazon fees but still matter

Your margin is not only Amazon's fees. Add the product cost, packaging, freight, customs duty, VAT or sales tax where it applies, and advertising. Most new products need paid ads to get early sales, and that spend often changes the picture more than any single fee. Our product research guide lists the full set of costs to check before you buy stock.

How to check the fees for your own product

  1. Open the current fee pages for your marketplace in Seller Central. Look at the referral fee for your category and the FBA rate card.
  2. Use Amazon's revenue calculator with your real product size, weight and planned price.
  3. Compare the result with fulfilling orders yourself. Our FBA vs FBM guide explains when each option tends to suit a seller.
  4. After you launch, read the fee details on your payments and order reports. Make sure the size tier and fees Amazon charges match what you planned.
  5. Check again when Amazon announces fee changes, which it usually does in advance.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Using fee figures from an old video or article instead of the current schedule.
  • Ignoring storage costs and sending several months of stock at once.
  • Choosing packaging without checking which size tier it puts the product in.
  • Never comparing the fees actually charged with the expected ones.
  • Leaving advertising out of the margin because it is not an Amazon fee.

FBA fees are not a reason to avoid FBA. Many sellers find the service worth the cost. They are simply part of the maths, and a seller who understands them can price, package and plan stock with far fewer surprises.
